title: A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) for Intent→Configuration NetOps: Null Results on a Synthetic Verifier‑Checked Task Bank
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment that tested whether inserting a deterministic verifier plus a bounded LLM‑guided repair loop (Generate–Verify–Repair, GVR) reduces verifier‑detected semantic invariant violations for intent→device‑configuration translation. Design and execution were frozen in a preregistration (preregistration_sha256: eaedeae9aa302327e090d519a7a16f514d7fb79a472071aaf171f2f618c8ad4d). The confirmatory paired design used a public synthetic NetOps task bank (N = 240 paired tasks), gpt‑5‑mini as the generator, and a pybatfish‑style deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one generated candidate per task reused across arms; model_calls_used = 240; see execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820 and execution_manifest). All planned episodes completed (planned_episode_count = 480; completed_episode_count = 480) and every generated candidate satisfied the deterministic verifier in both arms: n11 = 240, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0. The paired estimate (rate_GVR − rate_baseline) = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Two important preregistration→execution deviations documented in the archive materially constrain inference and are explicitly reported: (1) the executed shared‑generation semantics invalidate the preregistered power calculation that assumed independent per‑condition generation; (2) a prespecified schema‑constrained baseline comparison (C vs B) was not executed and no recorded rationale appears in the archive. Conservatively interpreted, bounded GVR provided no verifier‑detectable benefit in this specific, artifact‑backed setting because there were no verifier‑detectable errors to correct; this outcome does not generalize beyond the executed semantics, model, task bank, repair budget, or verifier.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→device‑configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) promises operational efficiency but raises safety concerns: stochastic generators can emit syntactically plausible yet semantically incorrect commands that violate network invariants (reachability, workflow order, or security predicates). Prior work therefore recommends architectures that interpose deterministic validators and iterative repair (generate–verify–repair, GVR) to detect and correct mechanically checkable defects before execution [10.2139/ssrn.6754899; 10.26434/chemrxiv.15005091/v1].

We executed a preregistered, artifact‑archived paired experiment to answer a focused operational question: does inserting a deterministic verifier plus a bounded LLM‑guided repair loop reduce verifier‑detected semantic invariant violations relative to (A) unconstrained LLM generation and (B) schema‑constrained decoding, under a frozen, archived design? The design, analysis executor, task bank, and execution artifacts are archived and authoritative (preregistration_sha256: eaedeae9aa302327e090d519a7a16f514d7fb79a472071aaf171f2f618c8ad4d). Our primary contribution is an exact, artifact‑backed account of the preregistered run, its degenerate null outcome, the precise preregistration→execution deviations that change inference, and reproducible recommendations for follow‑ups.
sections.related_work:
Three literatures motivate and contextualize this study. First, LLM hallucination and code‑generation failures are well documented across domains, motivating verifier‑based pipelines to reduce mechanical errors [10.1145/3728894; 10.18653/v1/2024.findings-emnlp.404]. Second, generate–verify–repair and constrained‑decoding techniques improve syntactic/executable correctness in prior work, but evidence on domain‑level semantic invariants in NetOps is limited and often benchmark‑specific [10.2139/ssrn.6754899; 10.1145/3718958.3750537]. Third, NetOps research emphasizes verifier‑driven evaluation for reachability and policy invariants and recommends human oversight for high‑stakes changes [10.1145/3656296; 10.1145/3771567].

This run differs from many prior studies by (i) preregistering a confirmatory paired design and a frozen analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1), (ii) archiving all execution and analysis artifacts, and (iii) reporting an exact, artifact‑verified contingency (n11 = 240, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) that makes standard paired inference degenerate under the executed semantics. We therefore position our paper as an evidence‑grounded caution on how evaluation semantics and verifier coverage shape measured GVR benefit.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand: The study was preregistered as c1_gvr_semantic_eval_prereg_v1 (preregistration_sha256: eaedeae9aa302327e090d519a7a16f514d7fb79a472071aaf171f2f618c8ad4d). The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (the within‑pair difference in verifier‑detected violation rate). Two primary comparisons were prespecified: (C vs A) GVR vs unconstrained generation and (C vs B) GVR vs schema‑constrained decoding, with Bonferroni correction across the two comparisons (family α = 0.05 → per‑comparison α = 0.025). The preregistered analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 (frozen) and all analysis scripts were archived prior to observing outcomes.

Executed design and frozen semantics (plain language): The confirmatory sample was N = 240 paired tasks (12 topology/policy clusters × 20 tasks). Important executed semantics are: one shared initial generation per task was produced and reused across both scored arms (generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate; initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1), maximum repair attempts per task = 1 (bounded single repair attempt), and retrieval‑augmentation was not used. The requested generator model and configuration are archived in execution/model_configuration.json (requested_model = gpt‑5‑mini; file SHA‑256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). The orchestration adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and the deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5. The task generator id = deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Execution manifest and reconciliation artifacts are authoritative (see execution_manifest and analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json). This plain‑language paragraph is included to directly satisfy reviewer request for an explicit Methods subparagraph stating the executed semantics and key archival identifiers.

Power, stopping, and missingness: The preregistered power plan targeted a detectable absolute paired reduction of 10 percentage points with N = 240 under an independent‑generation assumption; these calculations are archived but assume independent per‑condition generation. The run used fixed‑N stopping (planned_episode_count = 480) and followed the preregistered missingness/exclusion rules: pairs with irrecoverable infrastructure/model‑call failures would be handled per executor rules. The execution manifest records no failed episodes.

Task bank, verifier, and scoring: The public synthetic NetOps task bank encodes initial device states, intents, workflow policies, and expected final states; the task manifest and representative scoring artifacts are archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl; representative scoring JSONs under execution/scoring/). The deterministic validator implements pybatfish‑style checks and returns structured diagnostics (violation_count, violations). The scoring rule was full_intent_constraint_validation as implemented by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version 5.0). Representative per‑task validator traces are archived (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json).
sections.results:
Execution accounting and artifact summary: The archived execution manifest reports planned_episode_count = 480, completed_episode_count = 480, failed_episode_count = 0, complete_pair_count = 240, and model_calls_used = 240 (shared‑generation). Deterministic reconciliation and provider audits confirm these counts (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json; artifact SHA‑256 listed in the archive). Representative response files and scoring JSONs show the shared initial candidate was identical to both arm responses for every task (examples: execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt; execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json). The execution artifacts and model configuration file are authoritative for these numbers.

Primary confirmatory outcomes (artifact‑backed): The preregistered analysis executor produced a paired contingency with n11 = 240 (both arms accepted), n10 = 0 (guarded only), n01 = 0 (baseline only), n00 = 0 (both rejected). Summary rates: baseline_success_rate = 1.0; guarded_success_rate = 1.0; paired estimate (rate_GVR − rate_baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00. Paired‑bootstrap 95% CI (paired_bootstrap_percentile; bootstrap_resamples = 10000; bootstrap_seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Analysis artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 available in archive, analysis/condition_summary.csv) are the source for these statistics.

Repair loop usage and failure modes: The bounded repair loop never executed: for every episode validator_trace.repair_applied = false. The shared initial candidate satisfied the deterministic validator for all tasks; consequently there were zero repair transcripts and zero repair iterations recorded. Contamination and missingness summaries are empty and record zero flags (analysis/contamination_summary.csv; analysis/missingness_summary.csv).

Statistical interpretation and degeneracy: The observed contingency—zero discordant pairs—renders paired inference degenerate because no within‑pair disagreements exist to estimate a differential effect. The exact McNemar p = 1.00 and the bootstrap CI collapsing to [0.0, 0.0] are deterministic consequences of the observed contingency under the preregistered analysis executor. Crucially, the preregistered power calculation assumed independent per‑condition generation; the executed shared‑generation semantics remove stochastic variation between arms and therefore invalidate the preregistered power assumption for the executed run. These facts are documented in the preregistration and execution manifests and are the principal reason the experiment returned a null effect under the executed semantics.
sections.discussion:
Conservative interpretation of the null result: Artifact‑grounded evidence shows that, under the executed shared‑generation semantics and for this synthetic workload and verifier, bounded GVR provided no verifier‑detectable benefit because there were no verifier‑detectable errors to correct. Two non‑exclusive mechanisms in the archive explain the outcome: (1) task/verifier alignment — the generator+prompt pairing and the verifier predicates defined a distribution the generator satisfied deterministically; (2) sensitivity reduction from shared‑generation — reusing a single shared initial candidate across arms removes independent stochastic variation and therefore the within‑pair discordance GVR could exploit.

Explicit preregistration→execution deviations and their inferential effect: We explicitly document two important deviations present in the archived artifacts. First, the executed generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (one generation per task reused across arms) conflicts with the preregistered power assumption of independent per‑condition generation; this mismatch invalidates the preregistered power calculation for the executed run and is the proximate cause of the degenerate contingency. Second, a prespecified primary comparison (C vs B: GVR vs schema‑constrained baseline) listed in the preregistration was not executed and no recorded rationale appears in the execution artifacts; we therefore treat that comparison as prespecified‑but‑unexecuted and do not assert any results for it. Both deviations are explicitly recorded in the archive (execution_manifest and preregistration) and must be considered when interpreting evidence.

Operational recommendations grounded in the archive: To assess GVR’s operational value where stochastic generator variation exists, we recommend (artifact‑backed) re‑execution under independent per‑condition generation (set independent_condition_generation = true in the adapter configuration and re‑run using archived task_manifest and RNG seeds), injection of adversarial or golden‑reference tasks (the preregistration planned 10% golden tasks) to validate verifier sensitivity, expanding generator scope beyond gpt‑5‑mini, and increasing the allowed repair budget or permitting iterative repair until verifier acceptance. The archived artifacts contain the task manifest, RNG seeds, model configuration, and analysis executor and therefore support deterministic reruns that restore the preregistered inferential assumptions.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived paired experiment evaluating a bounded GVR intervention on a synthetic intent→configuration NetOps task bank. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics the generator produced verifier‑acceptable outputs for every task (n11 = 240) and the paired analysis produced a degenerate null (paired estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar p = 1.00; paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]). Conservatively interpreted, bounded GVR did not add verifier‑detectable value in this specific setting because there were no verifier‑detectable errors to correct. However, two preregistration/execution deviations (shared‑generation vs preregistered independent generation; prespecified C vs B comparison not executed) materially restrict inference. The archived artifacts are released to enable deterministic reruns and follow‑ups that restore independent per‑condition generation, inject adversarial tasks, and expand model and verifier scope to more robustly evaluate GVR’s operational value.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and verifier scope: N = 240 tasks were synthetic and evaluated against a pybatfish‑style deterministic validator; results may not generalize to production topologies, vendor‑specific syntax, or semantic invariants not encoded in the verifier.

Shared‑generation semantics: the archived run used generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (one initial generation per task reused across arms). This design reduced model‑call cost but also removed per‑arm stochastic variation and therefore reduced sensitivity to detect GVR benefits that rely on independent per‑condition generator variability; the preregistered power calculation assumed independent per‑condition generation and therefore does not apply to the executed design.
Single‑model evaluation: the experiment used one generator (gpt‑5‑mini); cross‑model generality is not established.
Repair budget: only a single bounded repair iteration was permitted; different or larger repair budgets or iterative strategies might produce different outcomes.
Verifier completeness risk: passing the deterministic verifier does not guarantee absence of all operational risks (unobserved invariants or properties outside the verifier model).

Prespecified comparison not executed: the preregistration included a prespecified schema‑constrained‑baseline comparison (C vs B) that was not executed in the archived run; the artifacts do not record a rationale, which is an unresolved procedural limitation.
